areas.name: Mount Lefroy
areas.blurb: Mount Lefroy is a glaciated summit of the Bow Range on the Alberta-British Columbia line, rising directly above Abbot Pass between Lake Louise and Lake O'Hara. Its usual route climbs snow slopes on the west side from the pass.

areas.name: Mount Birdwood
areas.blurb: Mount Birdwood is the highest peak of the Spray Mountains, on the east edge of Banff National Park above the Birdwood Lakes. Its ridges give long rock climbs well beyond the reach of ordinary scrambles.

areas.name: Mount Smuts
areas.blurb: Mount Smuts is a limestone peak in the Spray Mountains on the boundary of Peter Lougheed Provincial Park and Banff National Park. It is known as one of the most serious scrambles in the Kananaskis area, with very few parties summiting each year.

areas.name: Mount Cline
areas.blurb: Mount Cline is the highest peak in Clearwater County, a remote summit of the Cline Range north of Saskatchewan Crossing along the David Thompson Highway. It is a big alpine day or an overnight with a bivy at the tarns.

areas.name: Mount Northover
areas.blurb: Mount Northover is a 3,048 m summit on the Continental Divide on the Alberta and British Columbia border, standing at the head of the Three Isle, Aster and Joffre creek valleys in the Kananaskis backcountry. It is a serious scrambler's peak, usually reached from camps at Aster or Three Isle lakes.

routes.name: West Face via Abbot Pass
routes.rock_grade: Steep snow and firm ice on the face, with a short scrambly rock section near the pass; no true fifth-class climbing
routes.best_season: Summer, when the face holds firm snow in the early morning. Afternoon sun softens the slopes and sets off wet slides, so an early start matters.
routes.overview: The West Face is the easiest way up Lefroy, a high snow climb that starts at Abbot Pass on the Continental Divide. From Lake O'Hara the approach climbs steep scree and scrambly ground to the pass, then crosses a crevassed glacier basin before the snow slopes of the face lead to the summit ridge. Cornices overhang the east side of the top.
routes.beta: From the pass, drop onto the glacier on the north side and pick a safe line across to the base of the west face, roping up for the crevasses. Which of the gullies on the face is best depends on snow conditions; early in the day the snow is hard and crampons and an axe are enough. Climb the steep snow to the summit ridge and follow it to the top, staying well back from the cornices overhanging the drop to the east.
routes.approach: Bus or walk the Lake O'Hara road from the Trans-Canada Highway to the lake, pass Lake Oesa, and climb the steep scree and scrambling trail to Abbot Pass at about 2,925 m. The old hut at the pass has been demolished, so plan a long day or carry your own shelter. The alternative from Lake Louise goes through the Death Trap gorge and is exposed to avalanches and serac fall.
routes.descent_text: Reverse the route down the snow slopes while the snow is still firm, downclimbing with crampons and axes, then recross the glacier to Abbot Pass and return to Lake O'Hara.
routes.turnaround: Turn back if the snow on the face has gone soft and wet, or if rockfall and slides are starting on the west side.
routes.bail: Retreat the way you came across the glacier to Abbot Pass; the Death Trap gorge toward Lake Louise is a poor escape in afternoon heat.

pitch_detail.notes: Past Lake Oesa, then steep scree and scrambling that is exposed to rockfall and often holds snow or ice.
Rope up for crevasses on the glacier north of the pass and cross to the base of the face.
Firm snow in the early morning, climbed with crampons and an axe, up one of the gullies to the summit ridge.
Short ridge to the top, with cornices on the east side.

what_to_bring: Bus reservation for the Lake O'Hara road if not walking
hazards: Wet slides on the face in afternoon sun
Steep icy slope near the top
obj_haz: Afternoon avalanches on the west face
routes.watch_out:
Soft afternoon snow turns the face dangerous
The Death Trap gorge on the Lake Louise side is avalanche and serac terrain
pro_tips: Start early so the face is frozen and you are down before it warms
Cross the glacier roped and test the snow bridges
Stay back from the cornices on the east side

routes.name: Northwest Ridge
routes.rock_grade: Loose, exposed ridge climbing; a lower half of Class 3 scrambling and a few moves of 5.4-5.5
routes.best_season: Mid-summer to early fall once the ridge is dry. The crest is very windy and exposed, and snow or verglass on the rock makes it much harder.
routes.overview: The Northwest Ridge is the more commonly used route up Birdwood, ahead of the harder Lizzie's Ridge on the southeast side. It starts from the long Commonwealth Creek trail to Smuts Pass and then follows a narrow, airy crest of loose limestone to the summit.
routes.beta: From the high pass south of the Birdwood Lakes, turn onto the northwest ridge and follow it up. The lower half is a loose, exposed scramble that most parties find stays near Class 3. Higher up the ridge steepens and narrows, with a short knife-edge and a few harder moves in the 5.4-5.5 range; rock quality is poor, so test every hold. Many parties carry a rope, a small rack and slings for the harder steps.
routes.approach: Park at the road end near Mount Engadine Lodge off the Smith-Dorrien Trail, then follow the Commonwealth Creek trail through forest and meadow to Smuts Pass. Bears are common in the valley, and the trail is hard to follow where an avalanche brought down trees.
routes.descent_text: Descend the northwest ridge the way you came, then return along the pass and valley trail to the road.
routes.turnaround: Turn back if wind is strong on the crest or if the rock is wet, icy or snow-covered.
routes.bail: Retreat down the ridge the same way; the faces on either side are loose and cliffy.

pitch_detail.notes: Commonwealth Creek trail through forest and meadow, about 9 km to the high pass.
Loose and exposed scrambling on the lower half of the northwest ridge.
Narrow crest with a short knife-edge and a few harder moves on poor rock.

hazards: Verglass or snow on the rock
routes.watch_out:
Loose rock throughout the ridge
Strong wind can push you around the crest
pro_tips: Start early for a long approach and a loose ridge
Carry bear spray for the Commonwealth Creek valley
Move one at a time on loose sections

routes.name: South Ridge
routes.rock_grade: Exposed limestone slabs and a chimney at about 5.2, with a harder 5.5 line on the crest
routes.best_season: Summer, when the rock is bone dry. Do not attempt it when the rock is wet or snowy.
routes.overview: The south ridge is a long, committing route up steep limestone above Smuts Pass. A scree gully leads to three cliff bands and then a ridge walk to the summit. Many people call it a scramble but it climbs like low fifth class, and most parties rope up unless conditions are perfect.
routes.beta: From Smuts Pass, go up a scree gully to the ridge, passing the ledge system known as the Staircase. Three cliff bands follow. At the first the harder crest line goes at about 5.5, while the usual way takes a chimney to the right at around 5.2. Above, a ridge walk leads to the summit.
routes.approach: Park near Mount Engadine Lodge off the Smith-Dorrien Trail on the Mount Shark road, then follow the trail up Commonwealth Creek to the meadow between The Fist and Commonwealth Peak and on to Smuts Pass. Bears are common, and fallen trees hide the trail in places.
routes.descent_text: Descend the ridge until it drops steeply toward the col with Mount Shark, then down a west-side gully with short downclimbs and loose rock, followed by a ledge traverse to steep scree.
routes.turnaround: Turn back if the rock is wet or has snow, or if you lose the line on the cliff bands.
routes.bail: Retreat the way you came; the gully and descent drop away on loose rock, so rope up to descend if needed.

pitch_detail.pitch: Commonwealth Creek trail to Smuts Pass
pitch_detail.notes: Trail through forest and meadow to the pass.
Long gully up the Staircase ledge system and scree to the ridge.
Three cliff bands; a chimney on the right is the usual way, a harder line on the crest goes at about 5.5.

hazards: Loose rock and rockfall in the gullies
obj_haz: Wet rock making the cliff bands unsafe
routes.watch_out:
A solo fatal fall occurred here in 2018
The descent is harder than the ascent
pro_tips: Go with a partner and carry a rope
Spread out in the gully to avoid rockfall on each other
Start early; it is a long day

routes.name: Southwest Ridge
routes.rock_grade: Two exposed U-shaped notches at 5.4, with bolted anchors; otherwise scree, snow and easy scrambling
routes.best_season: Mid to late summer once the snow slope below the ridge has softened and the notches are dry.
routes.overview: The Southwest Ridge is the main route up Cline, a long approach with a small bivy site at alpine tarns and a ridge with two deep notches as the technical highlight. After the notches the summit is a straightforward walk.
routes.beta: Above the tarns, cross a faint headwall right to left, follow the glacial stream to a shallow col, and cross the snowy plateau to the ridge. The crux is two narrow notches in the ridge, each downclimbed and then climbed out of the far side at about 5.4. Fixed anchors and large boulders allow a rappel station if you want to protect them. Past the notches, a plain hike leads to the top.
routes.approach: Park on the grassy area across the David Thompson Highway from Thompson Creek Campground. Follow the creek trail about 4 km, crossing twice on logs, then climb the west moraine gully, a flagged route over a cliff band on a treed ridge, and a long scree slope past twin waterfalls to the tarns.
routes.descent_text: Return by the ridge, downclimbing or rappelling the notches, then retrace the approach to the highway.
routes.turnaround: Turn back if the notches are wet or icy or the snow slope is too hard without crampons.
routes.bail: Retreat along the ridge and down the approach; rappel the notches if needed.

pitch_detail.notes: Creek trail, moraine gully, flagged cliff-band route and scree to the alpine tarns.
Faint route across the headwall to a col and snowy plateau; ice axe and crampons for the snow slope.
Two narrow U-shaped notches on the ridge, each downclimbed and climbed out.

gear: Rope and slings for the notches
what_to_bring: Navigation for the faint headwall route
hazards: Snow slope needing axe and crampons
routes.watch_out: Notch conditions vary and the exposure is real
pro_tips: Consider a bivy at the tarns to split the day
Carry slings and a rope for the notches

routes.name: South Ridge
routes.rock_grade: Exposed 4th class on a narrow ridge with a harder chimney-like crack below the top
routes.best_season: Dry, snow-free late summer. Snow or ice on the ridge makes it far more dangerous.
routes.overview: The South Ridge is the usual way up Mount Northover, a 3,048 m peak on the Continental Divide in the Kananaskis backcountry. Easy grass and slab lead onto a narrow, exposed ridge with cliff bands and loose rubble, and a steep summit block finishes the climb. It is a serious, committing scramble with real fall consequences.
routes.beta: From the Aster Lake flats, head up grassy lower slopes and easy slabs to the start of the ridge. The crest narrows with big drops on both sides, broken by cliff bands and loose rubble. Near the top the angle steepens at the summit block; the hardest moves are a chimney-like crack just below the top, which can be avoided by a ledge traverse to a crack that leads to the summit. Terrain just off the line is harder than the route, so staying on it matters.
routes.descent_text: Many parties come down the same ridge. An alternative descent goes west from the south summit over steep, loose, exposed ground to a col and shoulder, then back toward Aster Lake; it is loose 4th class.
hazards: Severe exposure on the narrow ridge
Loose rock on the ascent and descent
Fatigue and route-finding errors late in the day
Snow and ice make the route much more dangerous
